endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Design the workflow, including the intervention that will be taken based on AI solution output

endorsements.title: A roadmap to implementing machine learning in healthcare: from concept to practice
endorsements.quote: To specify the intended actions that should be taken based upon a positive prediction, we work with the end users to leverage their expertise, values and preferences.

endorsements.title: Clinical problem selection for machine learning-based clinical decision support in the intensive care unit: complexity, actionability, and the way forward
endorsements.quote: First, is there a definable action that can be taken within the clinically appropriate time frame after the model’s prediction that is plausibly linked to an improved outcome?

endorsements.title: Cognitive Safety in Personalised Mental Health Nursing: A Structured Debates Essay on Minimum Viable Data for Safer Decisions and Lower Burnout Risk
endorsements.issuer: Journal of psychiatric and mental health nursing
endorsements.quote: Every displayed signal must specify: recommended next step, owner, timeframe, and link to the relevant workflow (order set/referral/escalation route); retire non‐actionable items

endorsements.title: A multimodal, risk-stratified framework for AI-driven early risk prediction and personalised prevention in obesity
endorsements.quote: Each tier specifies monitoring intensity, the AI-mediated intervention modality and the role of the human-in-the-loop.

endorsements.title: Clinical cognition in the age of cardiovascular AI
endorsements.quote: A risk score without a plausible action pathway is often an information burden rather than a cognitive aid.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing AI-Enabled Cardiovascular Biomarkers: A Clinician-Centered Framework for Validation, Governance, and Workflow Integration
endorsements.quote: A defined response pathway specifies the recipient; the threshold or conditions that trigger review; permissible actions; any required confirmation before treatment; escalation and de-escalation rules; when an override rationale is required; and how responsibility transfers across teams.

evidence.title: Long-term Effect of Machine Learning-Triggered Behavioral Nudges on Serious Illness Conversations and End-of-Life Outcomes Among Patients With Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: Serious illness conversations following risk-triggered clinician prompts specifying the intended action
evidence.effect: With the bundled intervention, high-risk encounter SIC rates increased from 3.4% (59 of 1754 encounters) to 13.5% (510 of 3765 encounters); aOR, 2.62 [95% CI, 1.84-3.72]; P < .001.
evidence.quote: Among encounters with high-risk patients, the unadjusted SIC rate was 3.4% (59 of 1754 encounters) and 13.5% (510 of 3765 encounters) in the control and intervention periods, respectively.

evidence.title: Spending Analysis of Machine Learning-Based Communication Nudges in Oncology
evidence.outcome: Mean daily end-of-life spending with risk-informed prompts for serious illness conversations versus standard care
evidence.effect: Mean daily spending was $377.96 vs. $449.92; adjusted mean difference, -$75.33; 95% confidence interval, -$136.42 to -$14.23; P=0.02. Adjusted savings were $13,747 per decedent.
evidence.quote: The intervention was associated with lower unadjusted mean daily spending in the last 6 months of life for the intervention group versus controls ($377.96 vs. $449.92; adjusted mean difference, -$75.33; 95% confidence interval, -$136.42 to -$14.23; P=0.02), translating to $13,747 total adjusted savings per decedent and $13 million in cumulative savings across all decedents in the intervention group.

evidence.title: Randomized Pilot of a Clinical Decision Support Tool to Increase Suicide Screening for at-Risk Primary Care Patients With Opioid Use Disorder
evidence.outcome: Completion of structured suicide risk assessment within 14 days of an eligible visit
evidence.effect: Adding suicide-risk alerts recommending CSSRS completion yielded completion rates of 20.3% versus 17.4% without suicide-risk alerts; OR=1.22, 95% CI=0.41, 3.65.
evidence.quote: Regarding the primary outcome, only 17.4% of control and 20.3% of intervention patients had a CSSRS completed at a visit in the 14 days after an eligible outpatient visit, with no significant difference between groups ( Table 2 ; OR=1.22, 95% CI=0.41, 3.65).

evidence.title: Perioperative goal-directed therapy with artificial intelligence to reduce the incidence of intraoperative hypotension and renal failure in patients undergoing lung surgery: A pilot study
evidence.outcome: Frequency and duration of hypotension with HPI-guided treatment versus no specific hemodynamic protocol
evidence.effect: HPI-guided treatment reduced hypotensive episodes: 0 [0-1] vs. 1 [0-2]; p = 0.01; and duration: 0 min [0-3.17] vs. 2.33 min [0-7.42]; p = 0.01.
evidence.quote: The number of hypotensive episodes was lower in the intervention group compared to the control group (0 [0-1] vs. 1 [0-2]; p = 0.01), the duration of hypotension was shorter in the intervention group (0 min [0-3.17] vs. 2.33 min [0-7.42]; p = 0.01).

evidence.title: Impact of Prognostic Notifications on Inpatient Advance Care Planning: A Cluster Randomized Trial
evidence.venue: Journal of pain and symptom management
evidence.outcome: ACP documentation by randomized physician after high-risk notification recommending ACP
evidence.effect: Intervention 34.7% vs control 19.6% (OR 2.04; 95% CI 1.16-3.59); no significant change in ACP documentation by any clinician (52.8% vs 42.8%, OR 1.31; 95% CI 0.81-2.13).
evidence.quote: Patients of physicians randomized to the intervention group were more likely to have a documented ACP conversation by the randomized physician compared to the control group (34.7% vs. 19.6%; OR 2.04; 95% CI 1.16-3.59).

evidence.title: Comparing clinical decision support systems for improving follow-up of abnormal cervical cancer screening test results
evidence.outcome: Follow-up completion when CDSS output paired with defined patient outreach action
evidence.effect: CDSS with outreach with or without navigation vs usual care: System A 38.2% or 37.2% vs 23.5% (p<0.001); System B 25.4% or 23% vs 19.7% (p=0.044). CDSS alone gave no improvement.
evidence.quote: CDSS with patient outreach with or without navigation versus usual care significantly increased follow-up rates in System A (38.2 % or 37.2 % vs 23.5 %, p < 0.001) and System B (25.4 % or 23 % vs. 19.7 %, p = 0.044).

evidence.title: Identifying risk factors for drug use recurrence with ecological momentary assessment, wearable technologies, and machine learning: a feasibility trial of peer recovery support specialist intervention
evidence.outcome: Anxiety, depression, stress, angst composite, and maximum craving following alert-linked peer outreach
evidence.effect: Adding PRSS calls to participant alerts modestly reduced anxiety, stress, depression, and angst composite (all p's < 0.001) and maximum craving (p = 0.011). Calls included random as well as anomaly-triggered alerts.
evidence.quote: Statistically significant reductions were noted in anxiety, depression, stress, angst, and cravings in the PRSS intervention arm relative to the SoC arm, though the extent of the differences was modest, therefore likely tempering the clinical significance.

evidence.title: Prediction-Augmented Shared Decision-Making and Lung Cancer Screening Uptake
evidence.outcome: Benefit-based lung cancer screening uptake before vs after category-specific encouragement tool
evidence.effect: Benefit-based LCS OR 1.03 preimplementation vs 1.81 implementation and 1.55 postimplementation; final-month screening probability 24.8% high-benefit vs 15.8% intermediate (difference 9.0 points; 95% CI, 1.6%-16.5%).
evidence.quote: This association was sustained, and by the final month of the study, the mean (SD) estimated probability of getting screened for a high-benefit person was 24.8% (15.5%) vs 15.8% (11.8%) for a person at intermediate (preference-sensitive) benefit (mean absolute difference, 9.0 percentage points; 95% CI, 1.6%-16.5%).

evidence.title: Implementing a Serious Illness Risk Prediction Model: Impact on Goals of Care Documentation
evidence.venue: Journal of pain and symptom management
evidence.outcome: Goals of care documentation before vs after workflow tied to risk-category outputs
evidence.effect: Documentation rose for high-risk patients (17.6%-70.8%, P<0.0001) and intermediate-risk patients (9.6%-28.0%, P<0.0001) after implementation.
evidence.quote: Postimplementation, goals of care documentation increased for high (17.6%-70.8%, P< 0.0001) and intermediate risk patients (9.6%-28.0%, P < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Pilot Study to Optimize Goal-directed Hemodynamic Management During Pancreatectomy
evidence.outcome: Intraoperative hypotension, cardiac index, stroke volume variation with algorithm-guided response
evidence.effect: IOH reduced 33.3% (5.2% vs 7.8%, P<0.01); cardiac index >2 up 31.6% (83.7% vs 63.6%); SVV <12 up 37.6% (73.2% vs 53.2%); groups differed in case mix; 10 PRE vs 24 POST patients
evidence.quote: There was a 33.3% reduction in IOH (5.2% ± 0.1% versus 7.8% ± 0.3%, P < 0.01, a 31.6% increase in cardiac index >2.0 (83.7% + 0.2% versus 63.6% + 0.5%, P < 0.01), and a 37.6% increase in stroke volume variation <12 (73.2% + 0.3% versus 53.2% + 0.5%, P < 0.01).

evidence.title: Human performance evaluation of a pediatric artificial intelligence sepsis model
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Antibiotic treatment of IPSO sepsis cases with versus without huddle intervention
evidence.effect: Antibiotic treatment was similar pre- and post-intervention without a huddle (9.3% vs 10.5%), but doubled with huddle intervention (22.7%).
evidence.quote: Treatment with antibiotics for IPSO sepsis cases was similar pre- and post-intervention without a huddle (9.3% vs 10.5%), though treatment doubled with huddle intervention (22.7%).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Algorithms Improve Care of Patients with AAA
evidence.outcome: Initial AAA evaluation after AI detection with defined referral workflow vs pre-AI
evidence.effect: Initial evaluation 42% vs. 18% (P < 0.001); evaluation timeline 22 vs. 83 days (P = 0.1); long-term follow-up 45% vs. 30% (P = 0.004)
evidence.quote: A greater proportion of patients underwent initial AAA evaluation after implementation of AI-assisted AAA care (42% vs. 18%, P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Integrated Implementation Strategies to Promote the Use of AI-Assisted Diagnostic Software for Lung Nodule Screening in China: Process Evaluation Based on the RE-AIM Framework
evidence.outcome: Completion and timeliness of structured referral following AI-assisted screening
evidence.effect: Referral completion was 88% (22/25); the median interval from referral submission to hospital visit was 3 (IQR 2‐4) days. Referral outcomes lacked a historical comparison.
evidence.quote: At the patient level, of the 25 individuals who consented to referral, 22 successfully completed the referral process by visiting the tertiary hospital, yielding a referral completion rate of 88%.

evidence.title: Perceived Trust and Professional Identity Threat in AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems: Scenario-Based Experimental Study on AI Process Design Features
evidence.outcome: Effect of specifying interventions in response to AI risk output on clinician trust
evidence.effect: Detailed preventive treatment advice increased trust (β=.262; P=.009) versus unspecific call for preventive activities; no effect on identity threat (β=-.072; P=.538).
evidence.quote: We found a significant positive association between an AI-based CDSS that is strongly integrated into the clinical workflow and trust in such a system (β=.262; P =.009), providing support for hypothesis 2A.

evidence.title: Randomized trial of electronic health record implemented AI risk prediction in kidney transplant care
evidence.effect: Clinicians reported a lack of immediate clinical consequence for the risk stratification as a main barrier to using the system.
evidence.quote: Users described the following reasons as main barriers to use the system: lack of immediate clinical consequence or no perceived need for risk stratification, lack of time during the visit, no direct integration into workflow since the integration was provided in another tab of the EHR, no alerts in case of high-risk scores.

evidence.title: From prediction to practice: early implementation of a machine learning-based hospitalization prediction tool in the emergency department
evidence.outcome: Absence of defined actions linked to AI predictions and effect on tool use
evidence.effect: Absence of linked actions was a reported barrier; 67% of staff reported rarely or never using the tool.
evidence.quote: Reported barriers included lack of electronic health record integration, absence of linked actions, and misalignment with existing workflows.
evidence.sample_unit: ED staff survey respondents and ED visits

commentary.bottom_line: Seven randomized trials in real deployments found that pairing AI outputs with a specified clinical action improved process or clinical outcomes in six, though most compared the bundle against usual care rather than isolating the defined response. One trial that separated the two found that decision support alone gave no improvement, while decision support linked to patient outreach raised follow-up completion.

perspectives.view: Seven randomized trials support high starting certainty, lowered one level for indirectness because most tested AI output plus a defined action against no AI. Trial 40935221 isolates the element and found no gain from decision support alone. A small suicide-alert trial was null (OR 1.22, 95% CI 0.41 to 3.65). Observational and simulation studies point the same direction.

In one trial, hypotension prediction paired with a treatment protocol reduced hypotensive episodes and their duration (p = 0.01), and a small pre-post study reported similar reductions. Two hazard studies found that clinicians avoided tools lacking a clear consequence. In one small trial, alerts recommending suicide risk assessment did not significantly raise completion (20.3% vs 17.4%).

Where risk categories were tied to a workflow, goals-of-care documentation for high-risk patients rose from 17.6% to 70.8%. Antibiotic treatment of sepsis cases stayed near 10% without a huddle and reached 22.7% with one. Initial aneurysm evaluation rose from 18% to 42% with a defined referral workflow. These pre-post designs lack concurrent controls.

A trial of risk-informed prompts for serious illness conversations reported adjusted savings of $13,747 per decedent in end-of-life spending. In trial 40935221 the gain came from outreach paired with the output, which suggests that the specified action may carry staffing costs that the software alone does not cover.

The largest trial included Medicaid patients and found that serious illness conversation rates rose from 3.4% to 13.5% (aOR 2.62). The only other trial reporting Medicaid enrollment was null and enrolled 115 patients. No study reported results for safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups.

When alerts triggered a call from a peer recovery specialist, participants reported modest reductions in anxiety, stress, depression, and craving, although some calls followed random rather than anomaly-triggered alerts. In a vignette study, clinicians trusted AI risk output more when it came with specific treatment advice (β = .262). None of these studies measured patients' own trust.

commentary.research_gap: Few trials randomize the same AI output with and without a specified response, so the separate contribution of defining the action remains uncertain. Studies have not compared ways of specifying actions (owner, timeframe, escalation rules), measured staffing burden, or reported patient-reported trust and access to a human.
commentary.underserved_note: Two trials included Medicaid patients: one large trial with positive results and one small trial with null results. No test reported safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the effect of defined response workflows in these groups is unknown.
